traditions/independent-catholic/summary: A loose movement of small churches outside the Roman Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican communions that claim apostolic succession through 'wandering bishops' (episcopi vagantes). Many lines derive from Arnold Harris Mathew, consecrated by Old Catholic bishops in 1908, from Joseph René Vilatte, consecrated by a Syriac Orthodox bishop in Ceylon in 1892, or from the Brazilian bishop Carlos Duarte Costa (1945). Theological positions range from traditionalist to very liberal.
traditions/independent-catholic/distinct: Claim of valid apostolic succession outside the large communions
Often married, women or LGBTQ clergy in progressive jurisdictions
Sacramental Catholic worship in the vernacular
Not recognised by the Roman Catholic Church as being in communion
traditions/independent-catholic/profile/: Varies by jurisdiction: typically Scripture, the creeds and Catholic tradition without papal jurisdiction.
Generally Catholic sacramental understanding of salvation.
Seven sacraments, often with open communion.
Small dioceses or jurisdictions led by bishops; many congregations meet in homes or borrowed churches.
Latin-rite (sometimes Tridentine, sometimes contemporary) liturgy in local languages.
traditions/independent-catholic/status: Active as hundreds of small, often short-lived jurisdictions; reliable aggregate statistics do not exist.
traditions/society-of-st-pius-x/summary: A priestly society founded in 1970 at Fribourg by Archbishop Marcel Lefebvre with initial diocesan approval, whose seminary at Écône trained priests in the pre-conciliar liturgy. Approval was withdrawn in 1975, and Lefebvre's consecration of four bishops in 1988 without papal mandate was declared by Rome to incur excommunication. Benedict XVI lifted the bishops' excommunications in 2009 and Francis granted SSPX priests faculties for confession (2015), but the Holy See holds that the Society has no canonical status and its ministers do not legitimately exercise ministry. The Society regards itself as fully Catholic, acting from a state of necessity.
traditions/society-of-st-pius-x/distinct: Exclusive use of the 1962 Roman Missal (Traditional Latin Mass)
Critique of Vatican II teaching on religious liberty, ecumenism and collegiality
Irregular canonical status: neither formally in schism (per many Vatican statements) nor in full regular communion
Worldwide network of priories, schools and seminaries
traditions/society-of-st-pius-x/profile/: Scripture and Tradition with the papacy and the pre-conciliar magisterium; the Society holds that some post-conciliar teaching departs from Tradition.
Catholic doctrine of grace, merit and the sacraments as defined at Trent.
Seven sacraments in the pre-1970 rites.
Superior General and General Council; bishops without territorial jurisdiction.
Traditional Latin Mass and Divine Office with Gregorian chant.
traditions/society-of-st-pius-x/status: Active, with several hundred priests worldwide; relations with Rome remain unresolved.
traditions/philippine-independent-church: A nationalist church proclaimed in 1902 by Isabelo de los Reyes and led by its first Obispo Máximo, Gregorio Aglipay, in reaction to Spanish friar control of the Philippine church. Early leaders drifted towards Unitarian theology, but the 1947 Declaration of Faith and Articles of Religion restored Trinitarian orthodoxy; Episcopal Church bishops consecrated its bishops in 1948 and the two churches entered full communion in 1961. It is known for its commitment to social justice and Filipino identity.
Filipino nationalist origins in the Revolution
Full communion with the Episcopal Church and wider Anglican Communion
Commitment to labour and social-justice causes (several clergy killed in recent decades)
Scripture, the creeds and Catholic tradition as summarised in its Declaration of Faith (1947).
Salvation by grace through Christ received in faith and the sacraments.
Creedal hope of Christ's return and eternal life.
Supreme Bishop (Obispo Máximo) with a General Assembly and Supreme Council of Bishops.
Vernacular Catholic liturgy in Filipino and other Philippine languages.
Active; one of the largest non-Roman churches in the Philippines.
traditions/church-of-sweden/summary: Sweden's national Lutheran church, which grew from Gustav Vasa's break with Rome at the Riksdag of Västerås (1527) and the preaching of Olaus and Laurentius Petri, and confirmed its confessional Lutheranism at the Uppsala Synod (1593). It kept a historic episcopate. A state church until 2000, it was among the first to ordain women (1960) and to approve church weddings for same-sex couples (2009).
traditions/church-of-sweden/distinctives: Historic episcopal succession claimed through the Reformation
Member of the Porvoo Communion with British and Irish Anglicans
Theologically liberal, socially prominent folk church (folkkyrka)
traditions/church-of-sweden/profile/auth: Scripture as the norming norm (norma normans), with the Lutheran Confessions of the Book of Concord as a faithful exposition (norma normata).
traditions/church-of-sweden/profile/salv: Justification by grace alone through faith alone on account of Christ, distinguished carefully as Law and Gospel.
traditions/church-of-sweden/profile/sacr: Baptism (including infants) and the Lord's Supper, in which Christ's true body and blood are present 'in, with and under' the bread and wine; private confession and absolution retained.
traditions/church-of-sweden/profile/esch: Christ's visible return, the resurrection of the dead and final judgement; amillennial in the confessional tradition.
traditions/church-of-sweden/profile/gove: Episcopal and synodical: bishops with a General Synod (Kyrkomötet) whose members are elected in church elections organised partly by political nominating groups.
traditions/church-of-sweden/profile/wors: Swedish High Mass (Högmässa), rich hymnody and choral tradition.
traditions/church-of-sweden/profile/cano: The 66-book Protestant canon; the Apocrypha esteemed for reading but not for doctrine.
traditions/church-of-sweden/status: Active; membership has declined steadily but remains just over half of Sweden's population.
traditions/church-of-norway/summary: Norway's Lutheran church, imposed by the Danish crown through the Church Ordinance of 1537 (applied in Norway 1539). Lay revival movements, especially the Haugean awakening led by Hans Nielsen Hauge (from 1796), shaped its popular piety and mission societies. Its formal state-church status ended with constitutional changes in 2012 and its separation as an independent legal entity in 2017.
traditions/church-of-norway/distinctives: Strong lay revival and mission organisations (Haugean heritage)
Bishops and a General Synod; separated from the state 2012–2017
Approved church weddings for same-sex couples (2016)
traditions/church-of-norway/profile/auth: Scripture as the norming norm (norma normans), with the Lutheran Confessions of the Book of Concord as a faithful exposition (norma normata).
traditions/church-of-norway/profile/salv: Justification by grace alone through faith alone on account of Christ, distinguished carefully as Law and Gospel.
traditions/church-of-norway/profile/sacr: Baptism (including infants) and the Lord's Supper, in which Christ's true body and blood are present 'in, with and under' the bread and wine; private confession and absolution retained.
traditions/church-of-norway/profile/esch: Christ's visible return, the resurrection of the dead and final judgement; amillennial in the confessional tradition.
traditions/church-of-norway/profile/gove: Bishops' Conference, diocesan councils and a General Synod (Kirkemøtet) with lay majorities.
traditions/church-of-norway/profile/wors: Norwegian Lutheran liturgy (revised 2011), hymnody in Bokmål, Nynorsk and Sami.
traditions/church-of-norway/profile/cano: The 66-book Protestant canon; the Apocrypha esteemed for reading but not for doctrine.
traditions/church-of-norway/status: Active; membership has declined but includes a majority of Norwegians.
traditions/evangelical-church-in-germany: Evangelical Church in Germany (EKD) and the union churches

The federation of twenty regional Protestant churches (Landeskirchen) of Germany — Lutheran, Reformed and United. Union churches began with the Prussian Union of 1817, when Friedrich Wilhelm III united Lutheran and Reformed congregations. The EKD was founded at Treysa in 1945 after the Church Struggle under Nazism, in which the Confessing Church's Barmen Declaration (1934) challenged the pro-Nazi 'German Christians'. The Leuenberg Agreement (1973) established pulpit and table fellowship among its traditions.
Federation of Lutheran, Reformed and United regional churches
Prussian Union (1817) and its Old Lutheran critics
Legacy of the Church Struggle and the Barmen Declaration
Church tax collected by the state
Scripture, with each regional church bound to its own confessions (Lutheran, Reformed or both); the Barmen Declaration widely received.
Justification by grace through faith, as affirmed in the Reformation confessions and the Joint Declaration of 1999 (on the Lutheran side).
Baptism and the Lord's Supper, with mutual recognition between Lutheran and Reformed understandings under Leuenberg.
Christ's return and the resurrection; modern theology has often reinterpreted traditional eschatology.
Federal: regional synods and bishops or church presidents; an EKD Synod, Council and Church Conference.
Lutheran and Reformed liturgies (Agende), strong choral and organ traditions.
The 66-book Protestant canon; the Apocrypha esteemed for reading but not for doctrine.
Active; membership has fallen steeply but remains around one fifth of Germany's population.
traditions/lutheran-church-missouri-syno: A confessional Lutheran church founded in Chicago in 1847 by German immigrants, notably Saxon Lutherans led by C. F. W. Walther, who had emigrated in 1838–39 partly to escape rationalism and the Prussian-style union. It subscribes unconditionally ('because', quia) to the Book of Concord, teaches biblical inerrancy, practises closed communion and does not ordain women. A 1970s conflict over biblical interpretation led to the 'Seminex' walkout (1974) from Concordia Seminary.
Quia subscription to the entire Book of Concord
Extensive parochial school system and Concordia universities
Scripture as the inerrant Word of God; the Lutheran Confessions accepted because they agree with Scripture.
Justification by grace alone through faith alone on account of Christ, distinguished carefully as Law and Gospel.
Baptism (including infants) and the Lord's Supper, in which Christ's true body and blood are present 'in, with and under' the bread and wine; private confession and absolution retained.
Christ's visible return, the resurrection of the dead and final judgement; amillennial in the confessional tradition.
Congregational-synodical polity with a synod president and districts; congregations call their pastors.
Liturgical worship from the Lutheran Service Book (2006), alongside contemporary services.
The 66-book Protestant canon; the Apocrypha esteemed for reading but not for doctrine.
Active; c. 1.8 million baptised members in the early 2020s, slowly declining.
traditions/evangelical-lutheran-church-i: The largest Lutheran church in the United States, formed in 1987–88 from the American Lutheran Church, the Lutheran Church in America and the Association of Evangelical Lutheran Churches. It ordains women (as its predecessors had since 1970), has full-communion agreements with Reformed churches (1997), the Episcopal Church (1999), the Moravians and the United Methodists, and in 2009 permitted pastors in committed same-sex relationships, after which some congregations formed the NALC and LCMC.
Ordination of women and LGBTQ clergy
Historic episcopate adopted through 'Called to Common Mission' (1999)
Scripture as the norming norm (norma normans), with the Lutheran Confessions of the Book of Concord as a faithful exposition (norma normata).
Justification by grace alone through faith alone on account of Christ, distinguished carefully as Law and Gospel.
Baptism (including infants) and the Lord's Supper, in which Christ's true body and blood are present 'in, with and under' the bread and wine; private confession and absolution retained.
